 WHO Director-General's opening remarks at the third IHR Emergency Committee meeting on Bundibugyo virus disease epidemic in the Democratic Republic of the Congo – 17 November 2026
 WHO Director-General's opening remarks at the third IHR Emergency Committee meeting on Bundibugyo virus disease epidemic in the Democratic Republic of the Congo – 17 November 2026
 17 November 2026 
 Remarks 
 Geneva 
 Reading time: 
 Chair, Professor Lucille Blumberg,
 Members of the Emergency Committee, dear colleagues and friends,
 Thank you once again for your commitment to this Committee.
 I also thank the representatives of the Central African Republic, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Kenya, Nigeria, South Sudan and Uganda for joining us today.
 Six months have now passed since this outbreak was declared, and three months since this Committee last met.
 In that time, the number of cases has more than doubled. More than 11 000 cases and 5400 deaths have now been reported, in 67 health zones across eight provinces.
 Children are paying a terrible price. They account for more than a quarter of confirmed cases and one third of deaths. Seven in ten children under five with confirmed Ebola have died.
 The risk beyond the DRC’s borders is not theoretical. Kenya has reported nine cases linked to an imported case, including two deaths. Its last patient has been discharged, and the 42-day countdown has begun.
 Nigeria has reported one imported case. In both countries, rapid detection and management of cases show the value of preparedness, transparency and swift control measures.
 I remain concerned that some countries continue to apply blanket travel restrictions. They hinder the response, damage livelihoods and discourage countries from reporting outbreaks quickly. 
 Targeted, evidence-based measures work better.
 There is also real progress. Rapid transmission has been halted in most of the early epicentres.
 At the start of the outbreak, two laboratories could test for the virus. Today there are more than two dozen. 
 Close to 2000 treatment beds are now available, and about 3000 people have recovered.
 And research is progressing. 
 Clinical trials of therapeutics are progressing, with more than 900 people enrolled; 
 Last month, a vaccine trial began using the Ervebo vaccine, which is approved for Ebola virus, but not for Bundibugyo virus. 
 Two candidate vaccines developed specifically for Bundibugyo virus will be added to the trial in the coming weeks. 
 But vaccines are not a substitute for the measures that save lives now: early care, contact tracing, isolation, safe and dignified burials, and trusted engagement with communities.
 But progress in some places is not control of the outbreak as a whole. 
 Between 400 and 500 new cases are still reported every week, and the outbreak is still expanding in some areas.
 When this Committee last met, I said that what concerned me most was where people are dying. That has not changed.
 Two-thirds of confirmed deaths are still occurring outside of Ebola treatment centres, which tells us that infections are being identified too late. Contact follow-up remains below target.
 Insecurity is now one of the greatest obstacles to the response. 
 Earlier this month, an attack on the town of Cantine-Aloya killed 66 civilians, including three health workers.
 Health facilities were looted and burned, and more than 1000 contacts were lost to follow-up.
 Two weeks ago a nurse was killed and another health worker badly injured when they were attacked while responding to an Ebola alert in Tshopo province. 
 These incidents restrict humanitarian access, disrupt operations, make it harder to reach communities quickly, and give the virus an advantage –  the virus can freely move while the response is restricted.
 Delays in paying frontline health workers and responders are also causing tension and slowing the response.
 And we must always remember that Ebola is just one of the threats these communities face, which means the response must also protect essential health and humanitarian services. 
 Outbreak control cannot come at the expense of primary health care, maternal and child health services, or access to treatment for other diseases.
 Once again, thank you all for your time and expertise.
 I look forward to your assessment of the situation, and to your advice.
I thank you.
